summary.text: For an odd prime, set \(T=2(p-1)\); Fermat’s theorem gives \(2^T\equiv1\pmod p\), so shifting indices by \(T\) preserves every product factor and, since the corresponding triangular exponents differ by a multiple of \(p-1\), also preserves the power-of-two coefficient, while each newly added term with index below \(T\) vanishes because its product contains \(2^T-1\). For \(p=2\), every positive-index coefficient is even and the sole remaining term is \(1\), so all values for positive indices are congruent to \(1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{\binom{k+1}{2}}
       \prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1),
\]
where an empty product is understood to be \(1\). Since
\(\binom{k+1}{2}=k(k+1)/2\), this is exactly the sequence in the statement.
We prove that, for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq 1\),
\[
 a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]

We first treat odd primes. Let \(p\neq 2\) be prime, put
\[
 q=p-1,\qquad T=2q=2(p-1),
\]
and perform all the following calculations modulo \(p\). Since \(p\) is odd,
\(2\not\equiv0\pmod p\). Fermat's little theorem therefore gives
\[
 2^q=2^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 2^T=2^{2q}=(2^q)^2\equiv1\pmod p. \tag{1}
\]
It follows in particular that powers of \(2\) are unchanged when their
exponents are increased by \(T\): for every \(m\geq0\),
\[
 2^{T+m}=2^T2^m\equiv2^m\pmod p. \tag{2}
\]

We will also need to understand what the shift by \(T\) does to the
triangular-number exponent. For every \(i\geq0\),
\[
 \binom{T+i+1}{2}
 =\binom{i+1}{2}+q(2q+2i+1). \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, using \(T=2q\), the difference between the two binomial coefficients
is
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \binom{T+i+1}{2}-\binom{i+1}{2}
 &=\frac{(T+i+1)(T+i)-i(i+1)}2\\
 &=\frac{T^2+2Ti+T}{2}\\
 &=\frac{T(T+2i+1)}2\\
 &=q(2q+2i+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the additional exponent in (3) is a multiple of \(q=p-1\). Fermat's
little theorem now yields
\[
 2^{\binom{T+i+1}{2}}
 =2^{\binom{i+1}{2}}(2^q)^{2q+2i+1}
 \equiv2^{\binom{i+1}{2}}\pmod p. \tag{4}
\]

Now expand \(a(T+n)\) and split its summation range into the indices below
\(T\) and those at least \(T\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
 a(T+n)
 &=\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}2^{\binom{k+1}{2}}
       \prod_{j=k+1}^{T+n-1}(2^j-1)\\
 &\quad+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}2^{\binom{T+i+1}{2}}
       \prod_{j=T+i+1}^{T+n-1}(2^j-1). \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the second sum is obtained by writing \(k=T+i\). We analyze the two
sums separately.

First suppose \(0\leq k<T\). Then \(k+1\leq T\). Also, because \(n\geq1\),
we have \(T\leq T+n-1\). Hence the index \(j=T\) occurs in the product
\[
 \prod_{j=k+1}^{T+n-1}(2^j-1).
\]
The corresponding factor is \(2^T-1\), which is congruent to zero by (1).
Therefore every summand in the first sum in (5) is zero modulo \(p\), and so
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{T-1}2^{\binom{k+1}{2}}
       \prod_{j=k+1}^{T+n-1}(2^j-1)\equiv0\pmod p. \tag{6}
\]
The condition \(n\geq1\) is used precisely here to ensure that the factor
with index \(T\) is present.

For a term in the second sum of (5), where \(0\leq i<n\), reindex the product
by writing \(j=T+m\). As \(j\) runs from \(T+i+1\) to \(T+n-1\), \(m\) runs
from \(i+1\) to \(n-1\). By (2), each factor satisfies
\[
 2^{T+m}-1\equiv2^m-1\pmod p.
\]
Thus
\[
 \prod_{j=T+i+1}^{T+n-1}(2^j-1)
 \equiv \prod_{m=i+1}^{n-1}(2^m-1)\pmod p. \tag{7}
\]
This remains valid when the product is empty, since both sides are then
\(1\). Combining (4) and (7), the summand indexed by \(i\) in the second sum
of (5) is congruent to
\[
 2^{\binom{i+1}{2}}\prod_{m=i+1}^{n-1}(2^m-1),
\]
which is exactly the summand indexed by \(i\) in the definition of \(a(n)\).
Therefore
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}2^{\binom{T+i+1}{2}}
       \prod_{j=T+i+1}^{T+n-1}(2^j-1)
 \equiv a(n)\pmod p. \tag{8}
\]
Equations (5), (6), and (8) give
\[
 a(T+n)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]
Since \(T=2(p-1)\), this proves the desired congruence for every odd prime.

It remains to consider \(p=2\). We first show that
\[
 a(n)\equiv1\pmod2 \qquad(n\geq1). \tag{9}
\]
In the term with \(k=0\), the power of \(2\) is
\(2^{\binom12}=2^0=1\). Every index in its product satisfies \(j\geq1\), so
\(2^j\) is even and hence
\[
 2^j-1\equiv1\pmod2.
\]
Thus the entire \(k=0\) term is congruent to \(1\) modulo \(2\).

For every remaining index \(k\geq1\), the triangular number
\(\binom{k+1}{2}=k(k+1)/2\) is at least \(1\). Hence
\(2^{\binom{k+1}{2}}\) is even, so the whole corresponding summand is zero
modulo \(2\), regardless of its product factor. Because \(n\geq1\), the
\(k=0\) term is present. It follows that exactly that term contributes modulo
\(2\), proving (9).

For \(p=2\), the proposed shift is
\[
 2(p-1)=2(2-1)=2.
\]
Both \(n\) and \(n+2\) are at least \(1\), so (9) applied to each gives
\[
 a(n+2)\equiv1\equiv a(n)\pmod2.
\]

Combining the odd-prime case with the case \(p=2\), we conclude that for every
prime \(p\) and every integer \(n\geq1\),
\[
 \boxed{a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\equiv a(n)\pmod p}.
\]
